subject: Career
title: Navigating Conflict Productively
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Navigating Conflict Productively.

hook.text: Two teammates disagree loudly. The manager avoids it. The conflict festers for months. Everyone suffers.

buildup.text: The Thomas-Kilmann model identifies five conflict styles: competing, avoiding, accommodating, compromising.

discovery.text: Most people default to avoiding or accommodating. Neither resolves the underlying issue.

twist.text: Productive conflict — task-focused disagreement — actually improves team decisions. It's personal conflict that destroys.

climax.text: Collaboration: 'We both want the project to succeed. Let's find a solution that addresses both concerns.'

punchline.text: Good teams don't avoid conflict. They make it productive.

quiz.question: What are the five conflict styles in the Thomas-Kilmann model?

details.summary: Productive conflict resolution focuses on interests rather than positions, separates people from the problem, and generates options for mutual gain. Most workplace conflicts escalate not because of irreconcilable differences but because of poor communication during disagreement.
details.whyItMatters: Unresolved conflict costs organizations an average of $359 billion annually in lost productivity. Teams that handle conflict well innovate more and build stronger trust.
takeaways: Focus on underlying interests, not stated positions in conflicts
Separate the person from the behavior when addressing issues
Seek solutions that create value for both parties where possible

faq.question: What is the difference between positions and interests in conflict?
faq.answer: Positions are the stated demands: 'I want this office.' Interests are the underlying needs: 'I need a quiet space for client calls.' Two people can have opposing positions but compatible interests. Uncovering interests opens creative solutions that satisfy both sides.

faq.question: When should I escalate a conflict to a manager versus resolving it myself?
faq.answer: Attempt direct resolution first using respectful dialogue. Escalate when the other party refuses to engage, when power imbalances make direct conversation unsafe, or when the conflict involves policy violations. Document your resolution attempts before escalating.
